utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I simply wanted to raise one scheduling matter and bring it to the Court's attention. This is a matter that has been discussed with Mr. Robinson and to which the Defence has no objection. As the Court will recall, the two witnesses scheduled to follow Mr. Ruez were Witness Todorovic and KDZ333. In order to ensure the completion of KDZ333's testimony this week, we have inverted the order. So it will now be following the completion of Mr. Ruez's testimony, KDZ333 and then Witness Todorovic, if the Court has no objection. As I say, there is no objection from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I want to move now to look at your final site, the Pilica site. If we can have 65 ter 2452 in e-court and go to page 20. Doctor, that's page 8 in the hard copy. Can you describe what this site was like when you first went there.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was just some new vegetation growing over the depression, sort of a depressed area, with the vegetation being totally different from the surrounding vegetation, but it was an area that had been dug previously if you go with some ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And what were the first steps that you took to investigate this site?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all we did a good surface search looking for possible remains, and we did find some, and then we were measuring the grave here, and then we began by doing transverse paths across that, digging down to see if there were remains were there, and we didn't find any until we got to the end, the far end. This would probably be dug by a big machine, and it ramped down in an incline and then got to the end. That was the end where we found the assemblage remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we go to page 42 in e-court now. It's page 30 in the hard copy of the report. Can we zoom in on the bottom photo. And, Doctor, if you can give us a sense of the size of the grave at this site.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that -- that point it was about -- it was 3 metres deep and you can see the edge of the grave is much higher than the individual standing there, so that was when the grave was pretty much emptied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And which part of the grave was the assemblage of bodies located in?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The far end. That -- when we looked at the original picture. We're looking at the end right now just -- with the previous photograph we had people measuring, and it was the furthest away from the roads that came -- the field roads that came from the farm itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you now just briefly summarise your findings for this particular location.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had 132 minimum count of -- 53 of the individuals we found were complete, 23 were nearly complete, and then the rest were body parts. They could be torsos, they could be legs, they could be individual bones, or they could be fragments of bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And that -- the number of 132 minimum number of individuals, is that something that was arrived at at the site or later at the morgue?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at -- it was at the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitchell. Doctor, your evidence in the previous case was admitted here in lieu of your examination-in-chief in addition to some supplemental questions by Mr. Mitchell, and you'll be cross-examined by Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Haglund. I should like to ask you for a precise definition of your professional position. What are you by occupation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm a forensic anthropologist. It depends upon where I'm working. I was an investigator with the medical examiner's office, so I did forensic death investigations as well as anthropology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is how you replied, that you are a forensic anthropologist and that you graduated in Washington. You said that in the Krstic case on page 3724. However, on page 9101 in the Tolimir case, you said that you were a forensic anthropologist and death investigator. Could you please explain to us more clearly what a death investigator is and how one acquires such a diploma, such a certificate.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: This wasn't a diploma. This was -- I -- I actually learned on the job when I worked 15 years with the medical examiner's office. And the -- what that involves is going to scenes, determining any mal-doings there. Oftentimes, we'd be working with the police. Especially on homicides we wouldn't -- the police would do that. But oftentimes we would go to a person that -- the place where a person had died of a natural death and we would just make sure that there was nothing that was out of place, that of -- for instance, in a suicide we would be looking for notes, we would be doing that, and collecting the medications, et cetera. We would try to get the -- the amount of time the person had been dead and -- and basically just look -- look through the house and especially the area where the deceased was before we removed the body. And if we had a problem where it was a homicide, then the pathologist would come and take the case from there, and we would stand by and watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, but in response to the question what your occupation is, when asked by Mr. McCloskey, when he asked you what your profession is, you said, "I'm a forensic anthropologist and death investigator." Is that your profession?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's my degree as an anthropology, but I do death investigations. I do assessments of graves. I set up the -- what's needed to do these -- these excavations and -- and set up the autopsy areas, make sure the individuals get to where they need to get, make sure that we have proper equipment, make sure that we have our -- our vehicles. If we were in a place like Rwanda, we need to take almost everything we have or else we wouldn't have it. We'd have to take our own cars, our own water filtration systems, our own bathrooms. So doing that kind of thing surrounding what -- what else we -- what else we have to do, but as -- as the person that's directing this, they have to be able to do these ancillary things also, but I am an anthropologist according to my -- according to my college education.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what you do, but I'm trying to find out what your training is. In the Krstic trial, on page 3724, you said, when asked what your position was, you said, "I was the chief medical investigator."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I worked at the medical examiner's office, yes, and -- you want to know what I did there? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. I'm interested in the training you got through education. Did you graduate from the medical school?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic -- Dr. Karadzic, if you wanted to know what the witness's training was, that should have been your first question. We've now spent 12 minutes to get to the question you really want to ask.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My schooling from college is anthropology, biology, a bit of archaeology, and then I went to -- and when the -- for the medical examiner's office, we would go to state meetings and to police teaching, and actually, I ended up doing a lot of that teaching, and they would have to do with the law as far as death investigation. It had to do with anatomy. It had to do with postmortem interval. It had to do with an area called taphonomy. It had to do with all of the kinds of work we had to do, and in fact, I co-authored a book that's used to train death investigators all over the United States. You have to know about medications. You have to know many things. But I am not a medical physician.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. With all due respect to you and the Trial Chamber, I'm trying to establish not all the kind of works you did but what you were qualified to do. Were you the chief medical investigator?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, but I worked underneath the -- the pathologist, the medical doctors. I worked for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So he was the chief medical examiner, not you; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not -- I was the chief medical investigator. The person that runs the medical examiner's offices usually are medical forensic pathologists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps it would be helpful to get a time-frame on these questions, whether we're talking about Dr. Haglund's role at the ICTY or previously. I think there's some confusion there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll come to that. I'd like to ask you since when have you been doing -- have you been engaged in forensic investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the Tolimir trial, however, on page 9108, Mr. McCloskey said: [In English] "He has been conducting forensic investigations since 1993."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was doing international -- international work on the kinds of topics that we're dealing with here right here in this Chamber since 1993, yes. And that's while I was working -- while I was working with the medical examiner's office, I would go on a foreign investigations in, for instance, Honduras and Guatemala, and also I went to the big grave in Ovcara and did some -- we did some exhumations in -- in part of the rest -- in the -- other part of the country there. So that was in 1993 was the first time that I went out to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You said that in the Krstic transcript, page 3725, saying that you took leave: [In English] "Well, I took holidays and went on some foreign missions. In 1993, I was a member of the expert committee and went to Croatia."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who established that committee?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN did, and the individuals that were involved in doing it were done by the Physicians for Human Rights. They're the one who put the team together, and I was asked to be on at that team. I didn't direct that team, but I learned a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this organisation is, doctors for human rights?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Physicians for Human Rights, and they had a forensic part that they did, but they did much -- they did much. They, in fact, got a very, very high honorarium for doing the torture of -- getting the first of -- I can't recall but it's -- I'm having memory problems so that's my big problem here, so, but it was -- but they did that. They look at other situations, and I think now they're involved with -- with Africa, with rapes of women, torture. They still do the forensic work, the work -- working in Afghanistan right now, and they do a lot of teaching.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but who are they? Who set them up and what kind of institution is it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a -- it's -- it's one that they don't earn money. They collect money from -- from the people -- people give them -- give them funds in order to run their -- it's -- it's -- it's not an industry or anything like that. It's -- it's called human rights. They do a lot of things for human rights. And they'll do publications and lectures and train people -- thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that's a private association of citizens in a certain line of work; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... Doctor, I don't quite [indiscernible] the Physicians for Human Rights got a high honorarium for doing the torture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not doing the torture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] I'm going to try to remember what it's called because it was a -- it was an international of -- thing that you get in Sweden. They shared that that year because they came up with protocols of dealing with torture and of -- and how to -- you know, talking about laws that should be in -- set in those things and what should happen about that, and actually the UN adopted that also, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did the UN adopt that protocol and in which document? Can you help us find it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't know when they adopted. I probably have it at home in my -- my library, but I don't have it in my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So nowadays they go around the world to investigate; correct? And their boss, the director of their pathology department, is Dr. Kirschner; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He's just part of the -- they had -- they have various groups working on different kinds of projects, different issues. One of the -- one of the groups within -- is -- is basically the forensic aspect of it. And a lot of what they do is -- is done with compiling information. They don't have to go around the world to find a lot of it. They compile a lot of information and work with organisations like Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch and things like that. And when needed, they would lend their forensic abilities to other organisations to assist them in what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Dr. Kirschner there at the time when you co-operated as director of that pathology department, or is he in that position still?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Dr. Kirschner was very sick at the time he was here and we didn't know it. He had cancer and he's dead. I took over his job when he died. Or when he was very ill and he couldn't work any more then I was asked to take over his job. So that's when I resigned from the medical examiner's office. Or that's when I -- actually I resigned from the Tribunal, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we'll get to that. Tell us, though, how did you get employed by this Tribunal -- or, actually, was it the Tribunal that employed you or the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was first the Rwanda Tribunal, and Dr. Goldstone had worked very closely at some times with Physician for Human Rights and he knew they had a long reach as far as being able to collect forensic experts to do things, and that's how I was asked to go to Rwanda to do the first assessments, and then when I was done there I came here and did the first assessments in 1995 and early 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So was there a specific document that employed you? Did Prosecutor Goldstone officially employ you before you went to Rwanda and before you did anything there, or was that done subsequently?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was done subsequently. In late 1995, about September, I took a six-week lay -- away from my work at the medical examiner's office in Washington State and I did the -- Physician for Human Rights paid for it. I did a lot of travel and that was paid for by the UN, but I did the assessments at that point. And then December 30th, I believe, or 31st, in 1995 then I was given a contract, and the contract was through the UN for the Rwanda Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when was it that you were engaged here at this OTP?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the first two large -- the two -- the two exhumations -- after the first exhumation, actually, I was asked to come up to The Hague and then go to the former Yugoslavia to start looking at graves that some of the Tribunal individuals were looking for or looking at, and -- and that's -- and then so I was bouncing back and forth between Rwanda and -- and the Tribunal, and it wasn't until early July, almost a year from the fall of Srebrenica, that I came back and basically stayed here for the -- most of the time and then started doing the exhumations and getting the teams and setting up the facilities we need, basically, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So what were the first two exhumations after which you were employed, actually?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first exhumation was the Cerska grave which we spoke of yesterday, and then subsequently the next grave was -- was Lazete. The next day was Nova Kasaba, and then we had to stop for about three weeks because the ordnance sniffing dogs had been taken on vacation and we had to wait until they come back, because I wouldn't take any people on any of the scenes without having at least inspected in a way that we would find out that there were no ordnance on areas, you know, so -- and then the last of the -- the next one was then Lazete and then the Branjevo Farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How is that possible? On behalf of who you or on whose authority did you work before you were actually employed by this OTP?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was working of -- I was being sort of supported by PHR, but I was working with the Tribunal, and I was working with, actually, Mr. Ruez. Actually, he was the person in charge of the Srebrenica investigations, and those were the graves that they were interested and wanted me to look at, so I accompanied them. When we were first doing assessments. I never saw him after we started doing the work. He was doing his own work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you Doctor, sir, I don't see who it was who authorised you to work on these exhumations. You do two or three exhumations and then only on the basis of that and after that you're employed by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was being paid by Rwanda, but I was working here, and then I think the second year and a half I was paid by the Tribunal. But Dr. Goldstone requested that. I come up from -- he was -- he was in charge of both Tribunals, and he asked me to come up here and I did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have to clarify that. Before you were employed here, on the basis of what did you conduct exhumations in Republika Srpska? On the basis of which document, whose document, which authorised institution?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the authorised institution I worked for was the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you were employed by the International Tribunal after the exhumations, not before them.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was employed by either -- by one of the -- one of the -- of the Tribunals from September -- late -- late December 1995 until mid-1990 -- 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have that document --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: What document is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- my contract? That's my contract. I had a contract with them, I guess. They hired me. I don't know -- I'm not sure what you're reaching for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Perhaps I can clear up this confusion, Mr. President. In 1996, the ICTR and ICTY had a single Prosecutor, and I don't know if that will assist Mr. Karadzic in moving on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the witness clearly said he was asked by Mr. Goldstone, who at the time was the Prosecutor of this Tribunal. I think you can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, with all due respect, this witness worked on a private basis without authority and without having proper engagement. He worked on several exhumations, and I cannot establish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's your submission, which is reserved for the later date, but witness clearly said he worked upon the request of Mr. Goldstone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was part of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that you were employed by this OTP after a few exhumations? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you first employed and did you then do the exhumations? In this OTP, that is.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I was -- after I was hired by the UN, yes. I did exhumations after that. I did assessments looking at graves prior to that. At least in the context of the Srebrenica graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, did you report to the authorities of Republika Srpska there, and did you receive their consent for doing all of that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you make an offer to them; namely, did you offer them insight into your work? Did you want to share your findings with them?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never approached us for that. We allowed them to come to the -- the Cerska grave to visit and they were welcome to do that. Otherwise, there was really no attempt, at least to me, to come, although when we did the Ovcara grave in -- in Croatia of -- the Serbs sent a pathologist and he was able to come over and he watched the autopsies and saw what we did and visited the grave a couple times, and that was fine with us. We were completely open if somebody would have asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So then, as for these remains that were exhumed in Republika Srpska, you would hand them over to Mr. Masovic -- or, rather, the other side; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- when we -- after the exhumations, we passed them on to the Bosnians -- Bosnians, and they were in Sarajevo at that time, and that's -- they -- they -- we returned the remains to them. They were their people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your task?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was my task?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically -- basically it was to do the -- the exhumations and -- and see that the examinations were done and getting a cause of death, and you can see from the reports. However, being interested in the families and giving the families support, what PHR did, it started a group in Sarajevo and started outreaching to the basic Muslim religious leaders and -- and the -- of the names of the people that ICT -- that ICRC had, the Red Cross --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I do not object, but I don't think the public has any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Serbian translation I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Should you repeat [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm happy to repeat it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have transcript. You may [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. As a person that's worked with the dead, actually, ever since I was in high school, basically because I had an embalmer's licence at one time, and I dealt with families all the time and I dealt with families at medical examiner's office and I felt that these families need -- we did not have to identify individuals. We just had to reach the -- the -- what we were looking at as far as identification, as far as ethnic, you know, things like that, and -- and -- but it was important for us and -- and a lot of -- because Physician for Human Rights was -- was actually paying a pittance to the people who came over and worked from all over the world, that we wanted to set up an organisation that would start working with the families and start collecting information about when they were last seen, although most of the stuff we got from that was from the Red Cross and then start reaching out to the families and start getting information about the individuals that they were missing and describing their clothes and describing as much as they could about their medical situations and -- and so that -- that went on for -- till about 1999. And during that time, we were able at -- on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. May I -- we'll get to that. I was interested in the general assignment, as it were. First of all, let us see who paid the Physicians for Human Rights. Who paid them, and who paid so little?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Physicians for Human Rights, these people -- or human rights people, basically they donated their time. These were -- these were individuals that Dr. Kirschner had worked with all over the world, and, you know, the anthropologists and archeologists where -- Dr. Clyde Snow was also involved in that and -- and so we got a lot of people we knew that -- good pathologists. But a lot of people they got were as far as -- archaeologists and anthropologist were from Central and South America because they had been doing that work since 1983 starting out in Argentina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But they did have some fund. Who gave them money? Who paid them?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they got a -- I think they got a -- well, how they get their money is organisations donate that to them. They get this money donated, and they had about a million dollars donated and that's how we got our equipment and then -- to Rwanda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, this general part of the task at hand, please let us take a look at the summary for Nova Kasaba and elsewhere. That is on page 4. And you say that in July 1995 -- I'll read it out in Serbian so that it can be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the benefit of interpreters and the Bench, it's better to upload that part. Did you refer to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- Nova Kasaba report --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- which was not touched upon in your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct, and we didn't tender the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, let --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, Your Excellencies, this is becoming part of the case through the Krstic transcript that has been admitted, so in a way it can get by that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We do not prohibit you from dealing with that part, but let's upload it. What was the 65 ter number for that? I take it it's a report of June 15th --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2451, 65 ter 2451. That should be the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 4 now. The summary, it's got to be somewhere. This must be page 3 then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Seven?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Summary. Yes, we've got it in Serbian. Page 8 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm unable to read this. It's sort of blurred. Ah, thank you. That's helpful. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is part of your -- your executive summary where you repeat these assumptions, right, or the prerequisites for your work? And these assumptions are that approximately 7.000 men and boys went missing and that the majority are suspected to have been executed. Was that the point of departure for your work?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was -- that was the sort of introduction to what the thing's about that of -- 7.000 was the number up at that time. And -- and I think using the word "execution," probably I shouldn't have done that. These are deaths, and I'll not there to prove they're executions or not, I'm just there to talk with the dead people and look at the area and find out what's going on, and it's up to the -- the Prosecutors to put a context in there. I talk for the dead people, not the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you say that 7.000 was the figure that was bandied about then. What was the total number of victims that was assumed at the time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a continuing thing, you know. It's going on still, and I know that 6 -- over 6.000 have been identified far, so it's going up, but I could only do so much in one year, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at the time the figure of 250- to 300.000 dead Muslims, killed Muslims, was the figure that was bandied about?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us, please, look at the second paragraph: "The purpose of the forensic investigation of these graves was to collect evidence for the International Criminal Tribunal," and so on and so forth. So collecting evidence. And it says here what that evidence is.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: What that evidence is? Graves, remains, how the individuals were killed, and all of the things I have in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that was done for the Office of the Prosecutor; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was done for them, but what is in the reports are basically what the graves and the individuals in the grave and evidence around the grave, that spoke to us, not -- not the Tribunal. They got what they found. They got what they got, what we actually had observed and collected. And they could manipulate that themselves or deal with it in trials, but that's what these reports are about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Collecting evidence for the International Tribunal; wouldn't it have been more correct to say for the Office of the Prosecutor? Wasn't it the Office of the Prosecutor that had employed you and co-operated with you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was working for the Tribunal. The head of the Tribunal asked me, yes, and I worked with the Prosecutor section, yes. I'd worked with them, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. You did not work with the Defence, because the Tribunal consists of Chambers, the OTP, and the Defence. Did you work with the Defence? Did you co-operate with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never asked to co-operate with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the process of collecting evidence, what did you do with evidence that would work in favour of some Defence?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was all turned over to -- to the Tribunal, actually, so -- that's who I was being employed by, but that's where it went. I would not have known where to send it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us be more specific. You handed that over to the OTP; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To the -- to the Tribunal. To the -- to the Prosecutor's office, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For your understanding, OTP is a jargon of the Tribunal meaning Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you think that you had sufficient data, sufficient information to view things that had happened correctly in order to be able to rule out prejudice?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to believe I had no prejudice. I -- like I keep saying, and it maybe seems like simple to you, but we collected information about these graves and the people in them, and the reports are about them, and it can be utilised in the context of the courts. That's what police do all the time and that, and it's up to the Court and there's -- to deal with this. Yourself and the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So is it correct that the first assumption was that these were victims from July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that until we started finding the connection between who was in the grave and when they went missing and identifying some of them. Then you get more of the idea of who they are. But at this time we know most of the people that had been in Srebrenica graves, or a great many, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Victims from July 1995, were you cautioned of the possibility that there were victims there from other times, and was your task to single out the victims from July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because most of these graves hadn't been added to. They were -- bodies were taken out, not more bodies put in or put on other bodies. They're not old graves. And then, of course, I did see, I think, one or two of the first flyovers from July, and we knew when those graves were -- were -- at least there was activity around the graves. But I saw none -- no indication of -- of bodies having been there from previous wars or previous burials. At that -- that didn't show up in what our findings were. I can explain sort of how you come about that, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What did you mean, Doctor, by "flyover"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was some aerial photography done. You've probably seen these and I only saw one of two for just the July thing. That's when we were trying to find the graves. Branjevo Farm is one I saw. It's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you exclude all those victims that might have been pre-dating those July 1995? In other words, did you determine the time of their death and the time when they were buried?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for instance, the -- the one from Branjevo Farm, we knew when the deaths happened. We saw the dead people out in the field, according to this flyover, and we saw the machinery and that for where the grave ended up being. But the only way that we could really get an idea on when these people probably died is when we would find some identifications, and maybe they had documents that were very, very recent or that they had been reported to the ICRC, once we had identified them, that they had disappeared in first -- first of -- part of July in 1995. It's become much more clear since then, but we had little to go on at that time, and -- but when you have remains in a grave and you have one person on the bottom and one person in the middle and another person on the top and these other people are all wrapped around him because they're not layered at all, then you know that these people were dumped in that grave about the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you discern between the victims that pre-dated July 1995 is one question. Another question, however, is whether you could discern those victims that died in July 1995 which were killed in combat as opposed to those that were unlawfully murdered.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Well, when you look at graves when they're 63 per cent or so blindfolds, people don't fight with their blindfolds on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did your hosts tell you that the combatants, even Serbian combatants, let alone the Muslim combatants, used to wear bandannas on their heads or head pieces and that those may not have been blindfolds?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to see that all these -- all these head wrappings dropped right down below the eyes and they were tied very tight in place for the most part. They didn't slip. They weren't hats or bindings on a head. They didn't go up or didn't go down. They stayed on the eyes. They were tied very tight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When soft tissue disappears from the skull, do they still remain to be firmly tied or could they move up or down?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: When these bodies are -- are together and there's no space between them, these things won't migrate from where they were. And, yes, you're right. If the remains was on the surface and turned to skeleton and the head is moved around, or something, by an animal or it rolls down a hill, yeah, you could -- could lose a blindfold, but not in the graves. It would be very difficult to do that. And they were photographed in situ before we moved them, so ... But there were often a lot of blindfolds that were -- were -- or a lot of cloths, rings of cloth with knots in them sometimes loose in the grave and you will see that in my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In a grave, can bones be fractured under the burden of all the other bodies and the earth that comes on top of them?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've never run into that before, especially these deep graves. If something happened on the surface, it's not going to -- bodies are, you know, a metre and a half, 2 metres down. You can drive a tractor over them and that's not going to break any bones, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you, any of your employers or your hosts in Bosnia, that in that area a war had gone on for 44 months and that there was daily fighting during that time? Did anybody tell that you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware there had been a war. Yes, of course. We all were. The world knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that under our law there is a process that is called sanitisation, which is a process to remove carcass and bodily remains after each battle?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the warring parties handed their fallen soldiers over to their families, whereas they buried the enemy soldiers in mass graves?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No doubt that that happens at times, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that during the first year of war, up to March 1993, in the territory under the control of the Muslim side there were over 1.200 people killed and buried in over 50 mass graves? I'm talking about Serbs who were buried in mass graves.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no doubt about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the hosts then tell you do not investigate this mass grave or the other mass grave because the bodies that were buried there were killed during the 44 months of the war? Did they warn you not to do something, not to investigate some place because they belonged to a different period?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't -- they didn't mention anything like that. I was not aware and I'm not surprised that there would be bodies like that. If we had dug them up, they would probably have uniforms on, and that would be another situation and that would be a different report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that according to Muslim sources, up to 85 per cent of their own soldiers never wore uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no doubt of that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they tell you that between 13.000 and 15.000 people, Muslims, from Srebrenica after the 11th of July, went in the direction of Tuzla and they were fighting all the time? Two or 3.000 were civilians, the other were combatants, and a lot of them lost their lives while they were trying to break through towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I get a cite for the claim that 2- to 3.000 were civilians and the rest were combatants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I had time, I would do that. However, we heard Mr. Franken who said that between 13.000 and 15.000 set out, and we saw reports of a Muslim intelligence agency in which it says that 10.000 combatants reached Tuzla, that they had passed through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question was: Among those number of people, what's the basis on your part to -- to argue that only 2- or 3.000 were civilians among them?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The basis is the fact that 10.000 were combatants, which was confirmed by the Muslims. On top of all those who were killed, 10.000 reached Tuzla, and we know that the column consisted of anything between 12.000 and 15.000 people and 10.000 reached Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When you would like to quote Mr. Franken, be precise, or just put your case to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will do that in my closing argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, I put it to you, sir, based on what we have heard in the proceedings so far, that 13.000 to 15.000 people set out in the direction of Tuzla, that one-third carried weapons, and that the Muslim side registered 10.000 combatants who finally arrived in Tuzla and that some 3.000 were considered to be lost during their breakthrough through the forest. Do you know all that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vaguely, yes. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the Serbs found those bodies in the forests, in the woods, and that they buried them in mass graves?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know, did you hear that in Bare about 600 bodies of people who died from shrapnel was found on the surface?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any of these things, so I can't really comment on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I put it to you that our Zvornik Brigade, which was entrenched and putting up defence, suffered more losses over those three or four days than during the entire length of the war, would you agree that the side that mounted the attack must have suffered even more losses than that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not into battle-field things like that. I don't -- I could see what happened or not. I don't know. I was not there. I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with me that the host should have informed you of all the possibilities so that you did not have all those ambiguities that you, yourself, very honestly admitted having?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you -- could you tell me more when I said that there were these ambiguities that I admitted having? Can you tell me where that appears or if I could review that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 3759 in the Krstic case, in answering Judge Riad's question.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the context of that? Could you please tell me that? Then I might be able to help you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's upload Exhibit P4310, 4310. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think this is a specific line of questioning that relates to whether the Branjevo Farm had been disturbed and whether Dr. Haglund was aware at the time that he did the exhumation, whether that grave had been disturbed or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. If doctor sees the transcript page, that will be resolved, naturally. So -- it's page 37.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If I could make it a little larger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll come to that. Hard copy, yes, it's coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as you see by my report on the Branjevo Farm, the Lazete grave was very, very -- it just shouted at you. You knew what happened there. And I really -- really couldn't come to a final determination of what I felt there. I think I gave a couple possibilities, and I just said I would just wait for further information to come, because I didn't feel that I -- it was ambiguous to me, and I didn't want to say something that -- it's ambiguous. That's how you -- it's ambiguous. I can't make a call one or the other. And I gave two possibilities and there were probably other probabilities too. But everything does not seem clear to me. Some things are ambiguous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that's a very fair conclusion on the part of a scientist. However, I'm asking you now if you had all the information about the war that had lasted for 44 months and that in July during the critical period of time there were a lot of dead who were subsequently buried in mass graves, would it have been easier for you to deal with those ambiguities and possibly resolve them?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, would I have to -- have to investigate and exhume the grave and find out what was going on. Some -- if you see most of these -- of reports that we're -- we're looking at, I was able to resolve most of the problems, and I came to conclusions. Each grave is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to call up the two previous pages, 3757, for example, and then 3758. Do you agree with me, Mr. Haglund, that it is a much easier job for a piece of machinery to split a body, to break a body in parts if that body is in an advanced stage of decomposition? Much easier, that is, than it would have been for the same machine to do it immediately after the death of that person while the body was still fresh, as it were.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with these bodies that are fresh and actually adipocered, they last a long time in damp places like some of these graves were. A big machine could do that. Whether it was fleshed, unfleshed, skeletal, all they have to do is just drop that big bucket right down there - it weighs hundreds of pounds - and they would just crush it. And if you're dealing with bodies that are more -- gone far beyond in decomposition, when you lift them up parts will drop off, if the bodies were in that kind of condition. So, yes, you have a good point, yeah. But it wasn't this way in these graves. They were put in there fresh, and any decomposition that happened came while they were in the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look. You are aware that things could have been different here. If you look at the page, you can see that from line 7 -- look at your answer starting at line 7. And then line 17 --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to read the paragraph before, if I could here, and then I'll read down. Could you put it back, put it down so I could see the previous question and that -- what's going on there. Thank you very much. It jumped off my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I note the time. I take it that we have a printout of this transcript, Mr. Mitchell. I was wondering why we do not have more legible ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We can upload a better quality version and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But -- but we'll take a break now. Why don't we hand over the transcript to the doctor so that he can read during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, please be mindful of the fact that we have a very important witness here who has produced four reports. Please look at the time that you have given me irrespective of the fact that I'm a layperson. I believe that any Defence would have a lot of work here in terms of examining this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would not spend in the manner as you did. We'll take a break for 20 minutes and resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Haglund, please look at the entire page. Can we scroll up to page 25. You say here that the bodies may have been collected from the surface with the help of machines; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we then agree that you say here: [In English] "They could have tumbled and maybe been torn apart"? [Interpretation] Is this something that could have happened if the sanitisation process took place months after those people died?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one flyover picture I saw were the bodies in the field, and they were moved to the grade, which was a bit aways. I had -- I think they were moved by a machine, and I think they were scooped up off the ground, and they rolled and some of them got cut apart and some got put in that pile. Now I know there are secondly and tertiary graves where parts of those individuals were not in that first grave, that group of individuals, but bodies that had been removed from that grave ended up in secondary and tertiary graves and part of those individuals belong to the people that were -- in the -- what part that I was able to -- we were -- out team was able to -- exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I may not have been very precise. This is my assumption: There was fighting. Some of those who died in fighting were discovered only through you four weeks later, and then machines were used to collect the bodies from the surface. If a body that was collected in such a way from the surface and you, yourself, mentioned the fact that there may have been mechanical collection from the surface, would it have been easier for such a body to be torn apart by such a machine a month after the death than it would have been for such a body to be torn apart if it was scooped by the machine immediately after the death?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you said that a body in an advanced state of decomposition is -- is easier to disintegrate, to tear apart, than a fresh body.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Usually if it's -- if it's decomposed, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, another possibility. Can we rule out the possibility that one sanitisation drive from one battle-field collected some bodies whole and tore some other bodies apart, depositing them in one location, whereas another group of bodies were collected elsewhere and placed in a different grave?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a possibility, but I think we know now that that's not true, because all the buses brought those people out the same day, but that's not part of my report. This is stuff that I learned afterwards I didn't know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who told you that, and how do you know that there were no people buried there beforehand? I'm talking in principle. I'm not talking about any particular grave site. How do you know that in each sanitisation bodies are not added to an existing grave?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure it does happen. If the bodies were out, you know, say, like, three weeks or so that you said, I think we'd see some difference. In a deep grave like that we would have been able to tell there was something going on. If one pile was in -- torn apart but wasn't -- they were -- they were sort of save underneath that amount of dirt and they were doing -- going through adipocere and not regular decomposition that you would on the surface, and I think if we'd seen another part of the grave that -- that looked really different than the one we did and it was that deep, we would have some questions about that. But, of course, we didn't run into any other -- other groups of bodies down there, only at that one. And I'm saying in general also, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But regarding Lazete 1 and Lazete 2, within Lazete 2A and B show certain differences. Did anyone ever give you the task to determine which grave sites would be related to sanitisation and which ones would be related to executions?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in -- in the Lazete grave, once that grave was opened, they got to the atmosphere, and I think that they could have -- they would have -- they would have decomposed a bit more and faster because of that, but if you look at the bodies still in there, they're in pretty good condition. It's just the parts that were pulled off and fell off that were different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there a single grave where the degree of decomposition is approximately the same across the grave? In other words, is it the case that there is a large range in terms of decomposition?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, there is a difference in the decomposition. The bodies that are in the mass, where the mass grave is, the bodies are together, they retain fluids from the bodies and -- and they're, like, sealed together. But when you go around the periphery of the grave, one part of the body may be sticking into that mass and maybe the legs or the head or one part will be sticking out all by themselves. They'll be more decomposed than the ones in the mass themselves. But throughout I found when these graves were in piles pretty much the people within the pile are going to be pretty much the same decomposition as -- or preservation throughout that mass. I could show you pictures of those things, those kind of things, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that the only explanation, or is it one of the possible explanations?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's when they're all dumped in together and--- at one time, yeah. I, offhand -- I'm not sure I'm clear on what -- what the question is, but they pretty main -- they maintain pretty well. I mean they're -- they happened in the Katyn graves. After some 1993 they were doing -- they did some exhumations, and those bodies are still -- have saponified tissue on them. It's amazing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about Katyn in Poland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question. We didn't have the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Concerning variations in the degree of decomposition, is the only explanation the one you just gave, that bodies were in a pile and that different conditions apply, or is it just one of the possible explanations?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one of the possible explanations. In -- in dry -- in a really dry desert, for instance, like in Iraq, you have bodies that have been in for a year or two, and they may be of -- they're -- they'll maybe get more like mummified because there's not a lot of -- I just happened to do one grave that they were -- they were sort of laying in a single layer, but they were mummified and they were rather deep. And when you talk about the Cerska grave, although -- and you can see that was a shallow grave, a lot of those bodies are partially decomposed and the bones are free and defleshed and some parts of the bodies are still there. It would depend upon if other bodies had been laying on top of them -- for protecting them from the heat and the sun and the warmed up gravel that was around them. So, yes, there are different environments where these -- where various different kinds of things happen to the remains as far as decomposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm waiting for the interpretation. When we take into account the grave -- was it Pilica where you found that the grave is 28 metres long and only 14 per cent of it was filled with bodies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of just the floor. It was of the floor of the grave, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your opinion, that's a primary grave; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us now try to establish what happened there. How did it come about that a grave 28 metres long of a regular shape was dug and then only 14 per cent of it is used? More precisely, did anyone warn you that somebody -- did somebody tell you that it could have been a trench that was later almost accidentally used to bury people?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not heard anything like that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you know that there was combat there and the positions shifted.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the -- of the combat situation in -- in the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I clarify? Is Mr. Karadzic citing to something in the trial, or is it his position that there was combat in Pilica, because I don't think we've heard any evidence that there was combat anywhere near this location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic, what did you mean by "there"? Did you mean that there was combat in the Branjevo Military Farm?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying the entire area is criss-crossed with trenches, and I'm asking the witness if he has an explanation how come a big grave like that was dug and then only 14 per cent of it is used? Did he take into account the possibility that it was once a trench that was then opportunistically used to bury people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We heard the answer from the doctor. Please move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this one mass grave, although we couldn't really call it a mass grave because there was only one body of an elderly gentleman was there, used to be a trench, and do you remember you found shell cases of a large calibre there from bullets that he probably fired himself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Before you answer, Dr. Haglund. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Which grave are we talking about now? The body of one elderly gentleman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- there, used to be a trench.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nova Kasaba, is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how that man died. He had -- well, I know how -- his -- he had a -- a blunt trauma to his head, and he was buried in a -- in a very shallow grave. I have no idea of who put him there or if he was connected to the other three graves that we have at -- at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you go there or did somebody give you this information? Were you there at the time of the exhumation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I was gone during one when the -- there was another grave found there that had six individuals in. One had 7, one had 19, 1 person in one grave, and then there were 6 in another grave. I think I was at the autopsy area that day, but I was informed about all the stuff when I came back the next day. And I can see the photographs and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We've heard testimony here from a man who attended the exhumation that that particular grave used to be a trench and has all the characteristic of a trench. I'm asking you now, do you accept the possibility that trenches, once captured --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are wasting time by not giving precise reference. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I was going to ask for a citation and also just for Mr. Karadzic's reference, point out if he's referring to Mr. Baraybar, there are two sets of Nova Kasaba graves. So those two sets of graves shouldn't be confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think this is Nova Kasaba 4 that I'm talking about, and you spoke about that in the Krstic trial, page 3765. In Nova Kasaba 4, you saw 19 bodies. And in another one, you found one. It could be Kasaba 4. I think one body was found there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have the transcript, Doctor, with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Krstic trial. It's 3765.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Who had no determined cause of death. Skeletal remains which is explainable because of the relatively superficial nature of the body compared to the depth of the ones that were fleshed at the same site."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He could have been in there longer. He could have been found decomposed somewhere and put in that shallow grave. I don't know. All I know is he had, I think, blunt trauma to the head, and he was skeletalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did they inform you that he was buried in a trench and shell casings of a large calibre were found next to his body, and they could have been fired only by the man himself?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't recall that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at this: The Trial Chamber put very interesting questions to you in the Krstic case. Look at page 3769. Judge Wald asked you whether they were placed that way, and you say -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us find the page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3773 should be the page and goes on at 3774.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And this is 377?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: 3773. [Interpretation] We can move on to the next page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your answer was not heard here, but Judge Wald wonders how it is possible for somebody to be hit by 20 bullets if that was an execution. How long does a man keep standing after being hit by a high velocity bullet from an automatic weapon?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Still I'm looking at 3773, and I'm trying to find that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then why don't we rely on the e-court. Let -- let us show the doctor the bottom of page 3773. You see Judge Wald's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if you're done with this page, let us know so we can move to the next page. Next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mm-hmm. May I stand up just a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I stand up for just a second, here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people that shot these people that were lined up along the other side of the road--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could speak to the microphone. Yes, that would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did that spray-type shooting. They stood with automatic weapons across from him with these people facing forward for the most part, and just spraying those people with shots. That's why so many of them were -- some of them were shot 20 times. And they could be shot again in the grave but some of them were probably still alive when they hold them in. So, yes, he could have 20 shots on him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the text to the bottom of the page. Is it the case that in Cerska, the grave about which Judge Wald was asking, the victims fell down a slope, according to what you determined?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: They either fell over the slope or had been rolled over after they fell. Maybe some of them fell in a row. They were rolled over each other, rolled down the incline.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's follow your answer from page 22 and now we can move to the next page. From line 22, sorry. This is your first answer; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that there had been or could have been opportunistic killing and opportunistic grave robbing and manipulation of graves and tampering by people who didn't know what was where?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: And where is this statement he's asking us. I guess our question is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm putting my question, and if you don't -- if you answer, I don't have to call up that passage. Were you aware that there could have been opportunistic killing there and that bodies may have been buried at different times?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were buried by machines that dug the graves, and there was one big smear. I didn't see any differences. There were tracks going over there and they were continuous, so ... I think it happened around the same time. It could have been separate episodes but around the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at your answer to Judge Wald's question starting at line 5, and your answer begins at line 9, and then let's read till the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] But one question --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said it may have happened at different times, yeah, you're right, you're correct. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see the bottom of the page. You say you are sure they did not intend to leave body parts and that was your impression. Can we see the next page?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. And the reason they didn't -- for instance, in the Lazete grave, that area, that drainage, driving those big machines there destroyed all the brush and grass. All there was was mud, and it was a continuos big area of mud. And we found that the graves alongside there, alongside the embankment going up into a small forest, when people came back, the people -- the people driving the trucks likely weren't the individuals that did the killing. They wouldn't know, and even if they took somebody back there that had been there, that surface was -- the extent of that surface of area that -- the potential grave, they wouldn't know exactly where those bodies were. It would look similar to them. They would get close to them, but they didn't know, but they're digging in there blindly. That's why they leave things behind. And that's why they missed some things. They missed Lazete 2A, and they miss this one, the Branjevo Farm grave, when the graves were being robbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So as we can see at the very beginning of this page, all of that is your impression; right? And please take a look at your answer to the next question starting from line 5. [In English] "Many -- I think there is many, many possible reasonable explanations we could make." [Interpretation] Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It could be done at night. It could be done with individuals who are not familiar with the graves. They didn't know the extent of the graves. There are -- yeah. There's not a single answer to these questions. It's dependent upon the -- it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just as that is uncertain, there is also the possibility of opportunistic killings; right? 3775 is the page reference. [In English] "There has subsequently been another Nova Kasaba grave that has been exhumed, and I'm not sure how many individuals. I believe it was less than hundred. I am not sure, but I think my experience with homicides basically is oftentimes, although there may be some systematic approach to some killings, some are more opportunistic and you have a smaller group rather than a larger group. It's as simple as that."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now can we establish the following: A grave of 28 metres, Pilica, was it dug first and were people brought there then and executed, or was the execution carried out first and were they then brought to that grave?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a question I cannot answer. I don't know an answer, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But then it is quite unclear why -- or, rather, how this happened. Why would somebody dig a big grave and have a small execution, or if they already carried out an execution somewhere out in the field, then they brought the victims there to -- to at that grave. Isn't that a bit perplexing? Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no I don't. I can't answer that because I don't know an answer. I haven't talked with these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us take a look at your report Lazete 2 from the introduction onwards. In Serbian it's page 13. Is it correct that Lazete 2 was investigated already on the 14th and 15th of April, 1996?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 13 of Lazete, what you said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's first page of executive summary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The last sentence --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The introduction. It says, Chapter II, "Introduction," and then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this is on beginning page or page 13, because page 13 is a ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Serbian, it's page 13. There is the introduction first and then the third paragraph says preliminary investigation at Lazete 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was prior to exhumations. This was when I was -- I came at that time to look at the site. There was -- the only digging that was done was we found an individual who was lying on the surface, and so we sort -- it was a skeleton, and we bagged him up and put him in a -- in a -- above where we thought the grave was and buried him so he would be there when we came back, because the animals would -- there was a lot of dogs and things around that -- we just want to protect that remains but we photographed where we got it from, et cetera. But we did not -- I had not much idea what was going on there until we opened up the grave. That was just sort of an assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the original English version says "Preliminary reconnaissance."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. It says "preliminary investigation" here in the translation, "istraga." I'm sorry, so it's a mistranslation and this is an official translation of that. However, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many times was Lazete investigated, re-dug? And what happened in April, is that authorised or unauthorised? According to our legal system that would have been unauthorised digging. Who was it that gave the order to have this carried out?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't -- all we did was bury a gentleman there, and I wasn't exhuming graves at that point.
