I do know we did -- when we did the exhumation in that part where the bodies had been robbed from, as I told you it was very wet and it was a very deep grave, and the water caused some collapse into that area where that robbed grave was, Lazete 2B, and it was dangerous, and so I made everybody get out of that grave, and we filled it up, and then when the grave in front between the road and the -- the Ovcara -- or Lazete 1 grave was done, I had marked in my report there were still bodies that -- there was one body -- I knew because the legs were sticking out, and so then they noted that and then they went back in and dug that and got, I think, 19 people out that we had to leave in there because of the danger of continuing the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So in April of 1996, this was carried out, the first probes. Then the first visit by Physicians for Human Rights was on the 19th of August, 1996, and that's when the first exhumations took place. Were you interrupted by the rain then?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I comment on that in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then at the end of 2001, the investigation at that particular grave was done or ended; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what it was. I think it was probably around that time. If you say it's 2001 and you have seen the report, you're correct. I have no idea. I knew it was a few years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please take a look at the next page. It says that this started on the 26th of August and went on until the 1st of September. The post-mortems were carried out in the temporary morgue in Kalesija under the supervision of Dr. Robert Kirschner, the director of the international forensics programme of the organisation called Physicians for Human Rights. So he was the director of that programme; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we please have a page reference when this kind of material is quoted? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So he was the director, and as I had asked, and I was told that he was not.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the director but he wasn't around most of the time when he would ask some -- one of the pathologists to be the director at that time when he was gone, but of -- I think he was there at that time, because this -- I'm not sure if he was there at the time. I didn't keep track of his calendar. I know he had to go back and forth to the United States and other places, an so -- but he officially was the director of the autopsy and the pathologist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the Registrar, it's page ending with 1643.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was this report submitted?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was submitted June 15, 1998. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He said Lazete 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it was concluded by mid-September. Wasn't it handed in at the end of September 1996?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. After I got done with that, I had 25 volumes of -- or 12 or 25 volumes to write, put together, and it took me a year and a half to get those, and I prioritised those four graves that were being done first -- or excuse me, the trials were going on where these particular things were upon. The Ovcara grape was the first one that I did. So that's why some of these things lingered for a long time. It's just that I can only stay up 14, 15 hours a day and work on these things, and I only had one helper to do that, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at the next sentence then that is repeated very often when the final conclusions are being drawn up about the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we please have a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's find the reference and then go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the same page that you mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 2 of the report, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Autopsies, examinations of victims began on August 26." That's the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We just -- further down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the benefit of the interpreters. Yes. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says that: "Finalisation of cause and manner of death as well as editing of final autopsy reports was facilitated by ICTY legal advisor Peter McCloskey. The pathology summary was written by forensic pathologist Page Hudson, M.D. Other contributing authors to this report are noted in the Acknowledgements (Section) IX, Volume I of this report." Mr. Haglund, in several of your reports you acknowledge Mr. McCloskey for his active participation in the establishment of conclusion on the cause and manner of death as well as editing final autopsy reports; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had to put that in there because I wanted people to be aware that he didn't make changes at anything. He just went around the world to see the particular pathologists. I had done particular cases, had them look it over, and if there was a change to -- made these pathologists made the change, not McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I saw that in your testimony in the Tolimir case. However, do you agree that -- this, that you are acknowledging him for is not really courier's work. That is a very fundamental way of participating in the work, and of course the OTP must find this embarrassing. So he did take part in this endeavour and was acknowledged by you, duly acknowledged; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I mean finalisation, he got the -- if there was a change or anything done -- this was up in the air at the time there was this investigation going on. He finalised it by taking it all to the doctors and having them look at the papers, make sure they were comfortable with it. If they weren't, they changed it. That was the finalisation. I don't mean he did anything to finalise it, but he carried all the things around the word being a finalisation to this, basically. I didn't mean that he signed anything or determined cause of death for anyone or anything like that, no. Maybe I mis-worded this in a way that don't make sense to some people, but it made sense to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It makes sense to the Defence, too, but we just have to have this established if that's the way it was. Please look at Serbian page 79. I don't know what the English page would be. It's before the blindfolds or the ligatures.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this in the same case that we're looking at here, the Lazete -- Lazete.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, and I'm looking now, just before -- what part? Could you please tell me again. I'm [indiscernible] [overlapping speakers] blindfolds. Okay, I'll -- I'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Serbian I have page 79, number 3, Lazete 2, external examination.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Let me get here and I'll find it here.

utterances.text: Number 3, external examination.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Two pages before the one that we see now in Serbian. Two pages before this graph that we see. [Overlapping speakers] This is 8, number 8. This is 7 and 8. Eight in Serbian, 7 in English. Could we have 3?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I have it. I have it. It's my problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the page number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forty-nine, I think that's where we are talking about [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we looking at the right page on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 48 is where the blindfolds are. That was the blindfolds. Is that what you wanted or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he refers to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It's not the right page in English. Number 3. Yes, yes. This is it. Number 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 48.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Forty-eight, right there. So what is the -- what is the question there about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And for the record, in e-court page 61, probably.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So your answer given to Judge Wald in response to her question about the possibility of different times of burial, please take a look at this. If we look at this range of decomposition or degradation, does that also open that possibility, if you will?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to look at her question if I could and see my answer. Are we still around 3775 or ... could you tell me where Judge Wald asked that question, what page it would be on the testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Her question started from 3773.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Continuing to 37 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. I just want to know what particular page we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3775.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [In English] "Yes, that's very interesting. They may have appeared at different times. I have no idea." [Interpretation] That was your answer.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been a short-term time, but yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about this conclusion from paragraph number 3, external examinations? Does it provide a range in decomposition, and is that your answer to Judge Wald too?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- yeah, there was that range, especially in -- not so much in Lazete 2A, but in 2B, yes, there was a lot of differential decomposition. There were bones. There were bodies that were semi-saponified. There was -- there was a range, but that was because of the opening of the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you, Mr. Haglund, that as a physician I would want to have a distinction made between a sanitisation grave and a grave that was the result of an execution, does that become one of the possible explanations of these differences in Lazete A and B? So that is to say burials after sanitising of the terrain, what you describe, these different changes now, and on the other hand, a grave after a possible execution. Would that be one of the possible explanations as well?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never considered that. I've always thought it was about the same time period but that, you know, there might be a little change. I'm not sure. That -- that I do not know. But now with identifications being made we -- we know when these people disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about these identifications?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me -- let me-- let me just also say the people that went in when it was drier, they feel that that was one trench and there were piles of bodies put in and then they were covered up and then another part of the trench would be filled. Now, I think that was probably their idea and I don't -- you've already interviewed that individual who was in charge of doing the second exhumation. He was from Guatemala.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us take a look at this. This is the sequence. There is an exhumation, bodies are handed over to Amor Masovic. They are taken for a postmortem either to Kalesija or Visoko; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- they went -- I think at Kalesija. It was just by -- it's a short way out of Sarajevo, or next to the -- where the US Army base was where we had it done, so -- and -- and then I would think that the 2002 would be done at -- at another facility which I had never seen, so they'd actually made another -- we were working in a destroyed clothing factory or -- and they -- they were able with much more funding to have a real stabilised place. That's why their -- that's why there's probably difference. I wasn't -- didn't think about that, but that's what happened I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What would have stopped Amor Masovic from placing on the table in the meantime the corpses that he already has in Tuzla, any corpses that he wanted to place on that table?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: What table would that have been? He had no -- he had no connection to our bodies till we turned them over when we were doing it in 1996. I'm not quite sure. And then when they did the other autopsies, they would have done the autopsies before they released them to Masovic. I'm not quite sure what you're trying to ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was the identification carried out? On the basis of DNA; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them were done probably in the late -- more towards the late end of 1990. Probably didn't start doing DNA, because I took the DNA samples to the United States. It would have been -- we didn't get identifications till 1996. Probably 1997, 1998, sort of. These were difficult identifications. They were done by mitochondrial DNA, which is, you know, more of a problematic thing, and -- but the other identifications that have been done by the group ICMP, and it's a -- actually a real DNA lab, they had two great big storage areas with about 4.000 bodies in each one, and they were -- they still are doing -- these are the people -- I don't know if they're near Tuzla. I think they're near Tuzla that -- where they have their -- their laboratories and areas where they do -- go over the skeletons and try to put pieces together. Now they can do that with the DNA. So I -- I -- I don't -- Masovic really had nothing -- I don't know if he -- I had no idea what he was involved with. I first met him and we made a deal, or we made an understanding of how these things would be transferred to the -- to the Bosnians and -- but what they did, I don't know, because I didn't go back there for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I put it to you that they were identified -- actually, the remains of a person who died in 1982 were also identified, and if I told you this, what would you say to that? How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. This is not something that you wrote. I'm putting this to you, and I'm telling you that a person was identified who died of natural causes in 1982, and you didn't do that, of course, what would you say to that? What would be your comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Dr. Haglund. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Again, is this a hypothetical question or is it based on the evidence in the case? And if it is, I'd like a cite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will submit the exhibit when we talk about ICMP findings. I'm now just asking the witness, because he was convinced that the bodies were not being manipulated when they were handed over to the Bosnian government, and I'm putting it to him that a person who died of natural causes in 1982 was identified as one of the victims of the incident that happened in July 1995. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that at all, but I know that some exhumations were done in cemeteries and could have been picked up there, but I don't know. We really don't have an answer to that. Interesting thing to think about, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And I think if that's the foundation of the question, then we'd actually like to see that exhibit now, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I intend to disclose it in a more systematised -- systematic form, and I'm now asking the witness whether he is aware of that. I'm going to present it when we discuss ICMP findings. I'm just asking the witness whether he was aware of such a possibility, yes or no. Can we go to the following page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We heard the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The following page. Summary number 8 -- number 8, summary of postmortem findings.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] Number 8. [Interpretation] I'll apologise. Let's stick to bullet point 5 before we move on. Go back to 5 for a moment, please. Could you discern and were you informed about the custom that even Serbs and especially Muslims wore bandannas? Could you discern between a bandanna and a blindfold? Could you discern between any piece of cloth worn around the head and a blindfold?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I'd have to review all the clothing. I don't -- I don't recall having seen hats on any of these individuals, but I -- so I couldn't answer that. I saw things on -- blindfolds on people, and then I saw other people's -- other cloth, the same kinds of cloth, the same shape that, if you took the blindfold off and held it out it would be the same shape. I just assumed that they were blindfolds next to people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, if the hosts had informed you of that and if they had shown you photos of combatants with pieces of cloth around their foreheads, that would have been of some help to you; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can we go to bullet point 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have it before us, "Pathology summary." He confirmed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [indiscernible] what document we're looking at here. Okay. So what -- the question is?

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.text: Well, it says here the bodies were from Srebrenica. Were you told that or was there a way for you, yourself, to establish that they were all from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, through the Red Cross. They were last seen in Srebrenica alive and not after that by the people that were there. And that was in the documents usually, I think, that ICRC got. They wanted to know where the person was last seen alive, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, they were not identified at the time; right? So you were in no position to tell who was who. Nobody was; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were not different than any other graves that I assumed and wrote that they were part of the Srebrenica people. That's where these people were all disappearing at the same time, and like that other information with the flyovers and things like that, we knew when the graves were made, so -- it's a good question though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In any case, if new bodies were added to a grave, to any grave, then the previous one underneath was already overgrown with grass; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean if you opened up a grave afterwards to put more people in or -- you're talking about putting more people in the grave after the first grave's done and grass has grown over the top, is that what you're saying? Okay. And you're saying that got dug up again and the grass got on top of the ones previously there -- I'm not sure I quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In response to the Judge's question, you responded that burials may have taken place at various times. For example, if somebody buried bodies in 1993 or 1994 -- 1994, could that grave already be overgrown with grass by 1995, and in that case would it have been identified as an undisturbed grave at that time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You'd have to get in the grave to find out if it was a disturbed grave. You know, the grass grows very fast, and if -- if -- I see -- I can't recall any of -- well, actually, the Cerska grave, there was a lot of plants that had grown up. You can tell that they were very young compared to the other area outside of the grave area, but it had grown up at the same time, so it was consistent with one burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at -- for the missing body parts and can you please look at the paragraph before that in your report. It would be on page 58. In e-court it would be on page 71.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 58.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It sayings here that pathologist description often concerned missing body parts, but this did not say whether the grave comprised the remains of at least one bone. Wouldn't this indicate a rather superficial approach to the task at hand to a rather not precise approach to the job?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The -- I think you're saying that the pathologist would have -- of -- of -- name missing parts or body parts differently than any other anthropologist did, and the anthropologist went through and got them all together and looked at what the pathologist had -- had done and they made it all one -- one approach, and so that they took care of that, actually. I can say that. Last line. And it's presented in the appendix of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now can we look at page 61 of your report? I don't know what the corresponding page this would be in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Seventy-four.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Number 2, digging or disturbance of the grave and removal of the body parts between primary burial and the forensic excavation. It says here: "Disturbance of the grave between primary burial and final exhumation process at least for shallow graves is traditionally the result of scavengers or exposure of the grave due to erosion. The activities of humans may also result in loss of body parts. Lastly, bones can disappear during the period of burial during -- due to diagenesis (bone deterioration)." That is your conclusion; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't run into any bone deterioration in any of the graves that we were in. I mean, the bones that were buried were in good condition for the most part. Albeit they were fractured and things like that and -- but we did see any. That was a general response to shallow grave question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have listed all the reasons in this paragraph. However, had you known that combat had taken place here and that bodies were buried in different times, would you agree that sanitisation may have fallen under the category "human activity"?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you're talking about sanitisation, about removing remains or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's cleaning the former combat ground and removing casualties from the site after combat.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of those graves that we did, that never came to my mind. There were no -- I don't think that there was anything to lead me to believe that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you exclude that possibility? Is there a way to exclude such a possibility?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you thinking that there was a battle and parties of both sides were buried in this grave? Is that -- are you talking about that or -- I'm not really sure. Or are you talking about one battle and people in it and somebody tried to remove them because they're their people and that was the only side that was buried? I don't understand the -- not quite. If you could delineate that for me a bit, clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put the Defence case to you: During combat, the side that controls the area buries its own victims with dignity in the presence of their families, whereas the victims that had fallen on the enemy's side were buried in mass graves. That's how we discovered 50 Serb mass graves in the area that we liberated in March 1993. And now my question: Do you know that the enemy soldiers, the enemy victims that are left behind in your own territory, do you know that after every combat they are buried? And when we're talking about grave disturbance due to human activity, would that be one of such human activities that would lead to the disturbance of a grave? Can you exclude that as a possible cause?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly don't know if every combat individual is buried. Yes. A disturbance would certainly have -- activities would lead to disturbance of a grave, but of -- I really feel confident of saying these are non-combats when they have -- blindfolded and their hands tied behind their backs and they're all intermixed and it happened in the same kind of time period. So, no, it -- it may pertain to some situations, but it certainly wasn't any situations I was involved in the graves of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your time is up, and I have to ask how much time would you need to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would be happy with an entire session but somehow I'm not hopeful. I don't think you'll give me as long as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Haglund, let me put this on behalf of the accused whether I'm correctly representing him or not. For the purpose of convenience, let's suppose a secondary grave. Would you exclude a possibility that the Serbs, when the -- burying the bodies of those victims brought the -- the other bodies who died at the field, battle-field, and buried together at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's a possibility that people could be put in another grave if they're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At the same grave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the same grave. That's possible, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure it -- it deals with these particular graves, but yeah -- yeah, I'm sure that people do that, yeah. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at quarter to 1.00. Mr. Karadzic, you will have up to half an hour to conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And do you have some re-examination, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Not at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we may continue with Mr. Ruez, albeit briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct. He's -- I believe he's ready. He's here and ready whenever Dr. Haglund concludes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope you know how old I am, Your Honours. It would be easier for me to continue with Mr. Haglund until the end of today's day and then continue with Mr. Ruez tomorrow. This pace is really killing me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Time is precious. We will continue with Mr. Ruez's evidence. Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that in the case of graveyards in Nova Kasaba, the autopsy report is somewhat lacking in terms of the description of injuries and traumas? To be more precise, only diagnosis were given without any descriptions that might be verifiable and based on which an expert anywhere until the world could draw the same conclusions?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were hundreds and hundreds of slides taken, and basically the autopsy information could be looked at by somebody else and they could compare those photographs with what the pathologist had to say. These are not ten-page, you know, pathology reports. These are hitting the high points, what they needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, do you agree with me that an autopsy report everywhere in the world should lead to the same conclusions? An autopsy report based on a postmortem which was done by the book, descriptions based on facts and based on the scientific procedure should lead to the same conclusion by any expert anywhere in the world; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I would think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, in Nova Kasaba all we see are diagnosis and not the findings; i.e., there's no description of the procedure which ultimately led to those diagnoses.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: They put down a cause of death. You're right. People could look at the photographs and see the -- we're talking about gunshot wounds for the most part. You can see these on the slides that we took of -- of the gunshots, and they're all categorised and are here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, the Defence needs to check that. The conclusions cannot be verified based on what the pathologists have provided us with.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'd have to take that up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it was clear before. Nova Kasaba is not in the indictment, and so this line of questioning has little -- little purpose. It's obviously relevant, but there are far more relevant things that could be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. He was informed of that factor, but we cannot exclude that line of questioning because it may relate to the credibility of his expert report in general. But given the limited time, I'm a bit disappointed, Mr. Karadzic, not to raise more direct and relevant issues with this witness. Yes, please carry on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one more question regarding Nova Kasaba, although I don't know to what extend it's not admitted, because it's in the transcript from Krstic. Is it true that only six ligatures were tied behind the back?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that says it, it's probably correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention just to a few more things from the grave known as Pilica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we are going to deal with Nova Kasaba, then we should be accurate. The report actually says 27 of the 33 victims recovered from the Nova Kasaba graves had their hands bound behind their back, and that's VIII in the executive summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we are moving to Pilica. Very well. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic, but be precise when --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I just want to say that it follows from pathology findings that only 6 were tied behind the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, Mr. Haglund, did you encounter any cases where the ligature is only on one hand?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. I'd have to -- I'd have to look at the -- at the -- the report, because it's been a long time since -- to remember all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at Pilica. Section D. Section D. Pilica; A, use of territory; B, distribution of remains; C, the nature and condition of remains; and D is the cover over the grave. It says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters would appreciate a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us find out the proper page and then continue. What page do you have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While he's being brought in, the Chamber will issue a brief oral ruling. In the meantime, let's bring in the witness. The Chamber will now issue an oral ruling. On 17th of January, 2012, during the testimony of Witness Pyers Tucker, the Chamber admitted associated exhibit at P4230, a summary of three intercepted conversation from March 1993, between, number one, General Mladic and the accused; number two, Vinko Pandurevic and General Milovanovic; and number three General Mladic and Vinko Pandurevic. In the relevant portion of his amalgamated statements discussing Exhibit P4230, Mr. Tucker says "I have been told this is the record of three conversations produced by Croatian intelligence services" and then proceeds to discuss how the intercepted conversation relate to a meeting he had on the 11th of March, 1993, with General Morillon, Branko Grujic and Vinko Pandurevic. The Chamber recalls its previous rulings that intercepts are a special category of evidence which, before being admitted, requires further evidence about their authenticity and reliability from sources such as the relevant intercept operator or a participant in the intercepted conversation. The Chamber considers that summaries of intercepts such as those in P4230 fall into the same category and therefore that Exhibit P4230 was not sufficiently authenticated for it to be admitted through Pyers Tucker. The Chamber thus reconsiders its decision of 17th of January, 2012, to admit P4230 and orders that the documents be marked for identification as MFI P4230.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we briefly take a look at 188 from this album, and then I'll be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.text: [Interpretation]
